title: How RAG finds the right policy passages
objective: Learners see that retrieval-augmented generation embeds the question and every document chunk as directions in the same space, scores each chunk by cosine similarity to the question, and sends only the k highest-scoring chunks to the model, so top-k decides what the model can see.

recommended.why: A 3D embedding space shows chunks and the question as directions on a sphere, so cosine similarity reads as the angle between them and the nearest neighbours light up.

alternative.why: Whether depth adds useful information: does the 3D space explain retrieval better than a flat map next to a ranked list of scores?

assumptions: The vectors are hand-placed synthetic 3D unit vectors chosen to illustrate the idea; they are not output of a real embedding model, which would use hundreds of dimensions
24 policy chunks in three topics (HR leave, travel expenses, IT security), eight each; one IT chunk about using a VPN in airports and hotels sits close to the travel topic on purpose
Similarity is cosine similarity: dot(q, c) / (|q| |c|); ties are broken by chunk order
Retrieval returns the k highest-scoring chunks with no minimum score and no re-ranking
units: cosine similarity: unitless, from -1 (opposite) to 1 (same direction)
top-k: number of chunks sent to the model
checkDescription: Every similarity equals the true cosine dot(q, c)/(|q||c|), the k passages sent to the model are the k highest scores in order, and for each of the three questions the best match comes from the matching topic.
expectAtDefaults: m.context.length === 3 && m.context.every(c => c.topic === m.question.topic) && m.ranked[0].title === 'Taxis and ride-share'

learnerPrompts.predict: On the taxi question, raise top-k from 3 to 5. Will every passage the model sees still be about travel expenses?
learnerPrompts.explain: The VPN chunk is about IT security, yet it can outrank travel chunks for a taxi question. What does that tell you about choosing k and about how chunks are written?
